supporting_evidence.summary: significant deviations in scope [all services]: emailservice_latency-90 z=6836.89 (34184.5%); emailservice_latency-50 z=1123.75 (5618.8%); emailservice_cpu z=543.47 (5938.5%); checkoutservice_latency-90 z=88.58 (694.2%)
traces for emailservice: SIGNIFICANT change; own spans self-time p50 0.2->0.24ms (1.16x), errors 0.0->0.0; inbound calls self-time p50 3.78->84.73ms (22.42x), errors 0.0->0.0

alternatives_rejected.why: A pure network delay would not raise CPU, yet emailservice_cpu rose 5938.5% (z=543.47) together with its latency (E1).

alternatives_rejected.candidate: checkoutservice: slowed only because it calls emailservice
alternatives_rejected.why: Its latency-90 deviation (z=88.58) is far smaller than emailservice's (z=6836.89) (E1), and callers saw emailservice slow 22x (E2), so checkout is a downstream victim.

proposed_fix.description: Find and stop whatever is consuming emailservice CPU, such as a runaway process or stress workload. Then raise emailservice CPU limits or scale out its replicas, and check that emailservice and checkoutservice latency return to baseline.

investigation.thought: No evidence yet; start with an unfiltered metric_query to rank every service and metric by before/after-alert deviation.

E1 shows emailservice has by far the biggest latency spike along with a large CPU jump, and checkoutservice latency is up as well. Checking traces for emailservice should show whether its own latency rose and whether checkout's slowdown is just caller-side, which gives the second telemetry kind I need.
Metrics (E1) and traces (E2) each independently point at emailservice, and its very large CPU rise alongside latency points to CPU exhaustion rather than injected delay.
